beats.text: Small animals. Young fish, crayfish, tadpoles, developing frogs.
They get a window, a few months without the things that eat them, to grow big enough that when the rains return and the predators spread back out,
they're no longer bite-sized. That window is not a nice bonus.
It is the engine. It is the reason the Everglades could support the enormous wading bird colonies it was historically famous for.
Every heron, every egret, every woodstalk in that system is ultimately eating animals that survived because of the seasonal reprieve.
Now watch what happens when you add an animal that doesn't have to leave.
The swamp eel doesn't need the deep water. It breeds air, so a drying pool is not a death sentence.
And when it does get too dry, it burrows into the same mud, in the same shallows, alongside the same small animals that were counting on those months of peace.
The predators are supposed to leave. This one stays.
It stays in the exact place the prey retreats to, at the exact time the prey is most concentrated and most vulnerable.
The window never opens, and that is why the tree frogs are still calling in Taylor Slough while nothing calls from the water.
The squirrel tree frogs, the green tree frogs, the Cuban tree frogs.
They breed in water, but they live above it. They spend their adult lives on trunks and leaves and branches.
In a layer of the ecosystem the eel cannot reach.
Eels don't climb trees. Everything below that line was exposed.
Everything above it was fine. The survivors weren't the strong ones or the fast ones.
They were the ones that happened to live at the right altitude.
And the numbers on what happened below that line had already been published, three years before Howell's amphibian survey.
In 2023, a study looking at the same system found that in areas the swamp eels had colonised, native fish and crayfish had fallen by between
85 and 93 percent. The authors described it as a complete ecosystem collapse, 85 to 93 percent of the small fish and crayfish.
Those are not incidental animals. In the everglades, they are the currency.
They are what the wading birds eat, what the larger fish eat, what the young alligators eat, what the amphibians compete with and feed alongside.
Take them out and you have not removed a species. You have removed the layer that everything else is standing on.
The 2023 paper covered the fish and the crustaceans.
What Howell's team did was go and check what had happened to everything else.
This is the part of the study that makes it hard to argue with and it's worth walking through slowly because the method is the whole reason the conclusion carries
weight. The team had their survey data, 2,251 amphibians, nine species, 30 sites.
They knew abundance dropped as you move toward Taylor Slough but correlation in a system as complicated as the everglades is close to worthless on its
own because there are a dozen plausible reasons for amphibians to decline and most of them are true somewhere.
So they built a model and they put every serious candidate into it.
Water level change over time. The Everglades hydrology has been re-engineered for a century.
Canals, levees, pumps, and drainage have altered how long any given patch stays wet.
Amphibians are sensitive to that. This is a genuine, well-documented driver of decline.
Soil nitrogen and phosphorus. Agricultural runoff enters the system from the north and drops off as you move south.
Nutrient enrichment restructures wetland plant communities and everything that depends on them.
This is real and in the early stages of the analysis it looked like the strongest signal in the whole dataset.
Disease. Chitrid fungus has devastated amphibian populations on multiple continents and is one of the most serious wildlife pathogens ever recorded.
Ranovirus does similar damage. Both were tested.
Pollution and other human cause pressures. Contaminants, land use, development at the edges.
Every one of those factors is a legitimate explanation.
